lines.text: The same customer, order and product, modeled three completely separate ways.
One question about them can be answered by all three. What differs is how much work answering it takes.
Here's the first question.
One of these models keeps a business key in a table by itself. Does that same table also hold what describes it, like a customer's own name?
No. Everything descriptive lives somewhere else entirely, on purpose.
That table keeps only the key.
Start with that simplest piece, confirmed.
A table that holds only the business key itself, nothing describing it, and barely ever changes.
Next, the relationship between two of those keys, kept in a table of its own.
Whatever keys participate in that relationship are exactly what defines its grain.
And finally, everything descriptive about one of those keys, tracked over time.
Nothing here ever gets overwritten. A change adds a new row instead of replacing the old one.
Here's the test.
If each of these three kinds of table gets loaded by a completely separate process, with nobody coordinating between them, is that actually safe?
Only if every one of those processes can work out the same key for the same thing, entirely on its own.
A shared counter handing out keys one at a time would defeat the whole point.
Watch this happen for real.
Two completely separate processes hash the same business key, never once talking to each other, and land on the exact same result. That's the entire mechanism, computed, not assumed.
Here's what that replaces.

A counter-based key forces a child record to go look up its parent's already-assigned key before it can even be written. Deriving the key on your own, from the thing itself, erases that dependency completely.
Now the actual cost of all this, measured rather than guessed at.

Asking for a customer's address as of a particular order's date takes one join in the simple normalized version, one join in the star-shaped version, and several joins plus an extra lookup once everything is split into separate business-key, relationship, and history tables.
That extra cost isn't an accident. It's the same decision, seen from the other side.
Splitting everything apart is exactly what made loading so easy a moment ago. Querying has to put all of that back together again, every single time.
Here's how that gets paid back down, also measured.
Pre-resolve that as-of lookup once, when the data loads, instead of recomputing it on every query, and one whole join disappears along with the extra lookup.
That trick works for one history table at a time.
When a query would otherwise have to cross several relationship tables in a row just to get an answer, a different kind of table pre-walks that whole path instead.
So what does all that extra querying cost actually buy you?
Nothing is ever thrown away, and a brand-new source system can be added as new tables of its own, without touching anything that already holds real history.
Three separate ideas, not one.

A business key, a relationship, and its history, kept apart on purpose. A key you can derive instead of having to ask for. A real, counted cost at query time, and two separate ways to pay it back down.
One more scenario.
A new source system joins next quarter, with its own version of the same business key. Which of today's three designs takes that with the least rebuilding?
The one built from separate business-key, relationship, and history tables.
A new business key just becomes a new table of that same kind, sitting beside the ones that already hold production history, rather than forcing a redesign of them.
